In the last few years, numerous conversations have been sparked about which Power Five school produces the best (x-position) players in the NFL. These questions began when it was noticed that Iowa (gross) produced a lot of the big name tight end talent, which lead other curious NFL fans to wonder what that was for wide receivers.
Today, I seek to answer that question by examining three different major schools and their wide receiver prospects from the last 15 years, from 2010 to 2025.
The contenders include Ohio State, LSU, and Alabama for funsies.


Code
ggplot() + 
  geom_point(data=nflWR_1025, aes(x=receptions, y=receiving_yards), color = "grey") +
  geom_point(data=lsu_wr, aes(x=receptions, y=receiving_yards), color = "purple") +
  geom_point(data=osu_wr, aes(x=receptions, y=receiving_yards), color = "black") +
  geom_point(data=bama_wr, aes(x=receptions, y=receiving_yards), color = "maroon") +
  geom_text(data=jsn_avg_nfl, aes(x=reception_avg, y=yard_avg, label = "Jaxson Smith-Njigba"), 
            color = "black", vjust = -1) +
  geom_text(data=jjet_avg_nfl, aes(x=reception_avg, y=yard_avg, label = "Justin Jefferson"), 
            color = "black", vjust = -1) +
  geom_text(data=cola_avg_nfl, aes(x=reception_avg, y=yard_avg, label = "Chris Olave"), 
            color = "black", vjust = -1) +
  geom_text(data=jch_avg_nfl, aes(x=reception_avg, y=yard_avg, label = "Jamarr Chase"), 
            color = "black", vjust = -1) +
  geom_text(data=obj_avg_nfl, aes(x=reception_avg, y=yard_avg, label = "Odell Beckham"), 
            color = "black", vjust = -1) +
    geom_text(data=jjo_avg_nfl, aes(x=reception_avg, y=yard_avg, label = "Julio Jones"), 
            color = "black", vjust = -.5) +
  
  
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1000, color = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 75, color = "black") +
  
  labs(
    x="Receptions", 
    y="Receiving Yards", 
    title="15 Years of Football, Only One WRU", 
    subtitle="LSU first-round WRs held more 'boom' potential in comparison to OSU and Alabama, though the biggest \nboom sprouted from Saban's crew.", 
    caption="Source: nflfastR | By Chase Wienk"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    ) 









As we can see in this scatter plot, a lot of LSU talent tends to land in the top-right quadrant of the chart, marking over 75 receptions and over 1,000 receiving yards. Major boom seasons from receivers like Justin Jefferson and Jamarr Chase from LSU. Each labeled name marks the titled player’s average reception/yard counts showing their productivity throughout their career. Julio Jones is a big outlier, that man was a simple beast who did not follow Alabama’s tendency to have receiver seasons in the bottom left quadrant.


Code
waffle(
        dWaffle, 
        rows = 3, 
        title="First Round Draft Spread", 
        xlab="1 Square = 1 First-Rounder \nSource: nflfastR | By: Chase Wienk", 
        colors = c("purple", "black", "maroon")
)









Here’s a simple one - who produced the most first-round talent at wide receiver?
That would be Alabama! Which would track given how dominant they were during Saban’s tenure as head coach. Julio Jones, again, was by far the best receiver Alabama contributed to the NFL. Another top pick from Alabama was Heisman DeVonta Smith - even though his career has not been as decorated in the NFL as it was in college. Aside from this though, OSU has emerged very recently as a top contender for WRU, sending all five of their picks to the NFL in the last four years. Overall though, LSU has sent the most productive receivers. From OBJ to Malik Nabers the LSU first-rounders take the prize.


Code
ggplot() + 
  geom_point(
    data=wru_wr, 
    aes(x=receptions, y=receiving_yards, size=ypr),
    alpha = 0.3) + 
  scale_size(range = c(1, 10), name="Yards per Reception") +
  
  geom_point(
    data=lsu_wr, 
    aes(x=receptions, y=receiving_yards, size=ypr), 
    color="purple", alpha = 0.5) +
  
  geom_point(
    data=osu_wr, 
    aes(x=receptions, y=receiving_yards, size=ypr), 
    color="black", alpha = 0.5) +
  
  geom_point(
    data=bama_wr, 
    aes(x=receptions, y=receiving_yards, size=ypr), 
    color="maroon", alpha = 0.5) +
  
  labs(
    x="Receptions", 
    y="Receiving Yards", 
    title="OSU Receivers Need to Step It Up to be WRU", 
    subtitle="While an emerging school with talent, a lot of the notable OSU receivers have come remotely close to rivaling \nthe summits of LSU and Bama receivers.", 
    caption="Source: Data Provider | By Your Name"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    ) 









Here we can examine the average yards per reception in relation to how many receptions and yards each receiver has in a season. In purple we have LSU, in maroon we have Alabama, and in black we have Ohio State. In here we can see that Ohio State has overall more relatively underwhelming receivers than the other two. An important point to note about this is that a large portion of these player seasons all hover around that 10-15 yards per reception mark. In general though, for my argument that LSU is the WRU follow in this graph as well. LSU has had the most impactful receivers in the NFL in comparison to these other juggernaut schools given their tendency to boom more than they bust. A very large piece of that argument comes from both Justin Jefferson and Jamarr Chase providing the NFL with several top-caliber receiving seasons between the two on their own respective teams. Aside from Jaxson Smith-Njigba and his start to this 2025 season, other Ohio State receivers have not stacked up to those two’s success.
Julio Jones had larger peaks than both of those LSU guys, however he is now retired and I feel as he was simply just a specimen on his own - not totally indicative of Alabama’s success in developing NFL-leading receivers.
